title: Bash Scripting Fundamentals: From Shebang and Quoting to a Failed-SSH Triage Script
intro: A Bash script is a text file of shell commands that the Bash interpreter executes in order, turning a manual procedure into a repeatable, reviewable one. In this lesson you will learn to write, run, debug and harden Bash scripts, from the shebang and the quoting rules through tests, loops, functions and arrays, ending with a complete SOC script that counts failed SSH logins per source IP and flags heavy hitters.

sections.heading: What a script is and how it runs
sections.content:
A shell script is a plain text file containing the same commands you would type at a prompt. Nothing is compiled: the interpreter reads the file from top to bottom and executes each line. For an analyst the value is repeatability. The same triage steps run identically at 03:00 and at 15:00, and a colleague can read exactly what was done.

### The shebang

The first line of a script should be the shebang, the two characters `#!` followed by the interpreter path:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# hello.sh - minimal example
echo "Running on $(hostname) as $(whoami)"
```

When you execute the file, the kernel reads that first line, starts the named program, and hands it the script path. Using `/usr/bin/env bash` asks `env` to find Bash on PATH, which works whether Bash lives in /bin, /usr/bin or /usr/local/bin. A hard-coded `#!/bin/bash` is also fine when you control every target host.

Pitfalls with the shebang:

- It must be line 1, byte 1. A blank line or a leading space before it makes it just a comment.
- Scripts edited on Windows may carry CRLF line endings. The kernel then looks for an interpreter literally named "bash" followed by a carriage return and fails with "bad interpreter: No such file or directory". Convert with `dos2unix`.
- With no shebang, the launching shell guesses. On Debian and Ubuntu the guess is often `dash`, which has no `[[`, no arrays and no `(( ))`. A script that "worked on my machine" then breaks in cron.

### Three ways to run it

```bash
chmod +x hello.sh   # set the execute bit (the permission model itself is a separate lesson)
./hello.sh          # kernel reads the shebang and launches Bash
bash hello.sh       # you pick the interpreter; no execute bit or shebang needed
source hello.sh     # same as: . hello.sh
```

| Method | Needs +x | Uses shebang | Runs in |
|---|---|---|---|
| ./hello.sh | yes | yes | a child process |
| bash hello.sh | no | no, you named Bash | a child process |
| source hello.sh | no | no | your current shell |

Because a normal run happens in a child process, a `cd` or a variable assignment inside the script disappears when it ends. Sourcing is the opposite: it is how you load helper functions or environment settings into your own session.

### Why PATH matters

Typing `hello.sh` alone gives "command not found". For a bare name the shell searches only the directories listed in PATH, left to right, and the first match wins. The current directory is deliberately not on PATH, so `./` is needed: a name containing a slash means "use exactly this path, do not search".

```bash
echo "$PATH"                      # colon-separated list of directories
mkdir -p ~/bin && cp hello.sh ~/bin/
export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"     # prepend your own bin directory
type -a hello.sh                  # shows which file would actually run
```

Two security points. Never add `.` or an empty element to PATH, and treat a user-writable directory early in PATH as a hijack risk: a file named `ls` dropped there runs instead of the real one. Also, cron and sudo start with a minimal PATH, so production scripts either call tools by full path or set `PATH=/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin` near the top.

sections.heading: Variables and quoting
sections.content:
Quoting is the single most important skill in shell scripting, and the source of most script bugs and many injection flaws.

### Assignment and expansion

Assign with no spaces around the equals sign. Read with a dollar sign, preferably with braces:

```bash
host=web01              # correct
host = web01            # WRONG: runs a command named host with two arguments
today=$(date +%F)       # command substitution: capture output
log="/var/log/${host}_${today}.log"   # braces mark where the name ends
```

Without braces, `$host_$today` would look for variables named `host_` and `today`. Use `$(...)` for command substitution rather than old backticks, because it nests cleanly and is readable. Useful parameter expansions:

```bash
echo "${name:-guest}"      # default if unset or empty
echo "${dir:?must be set}" # abort with message if unset or empty
echo "${#name}"            # length of the value
file=/var/log/auth.log.1
echo "${file##*/}"         # strip longest prefix match: auth.log.1
echo "${file%.1}"          # strip shortest suffix match: /var/log/auth.log
```

### The three quoting forms

| Form | Variables expanded | Command substitution | Word splitting and globbing | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| "double quotes" | yes | yes | no, stays one word | almost everything |
| 'single quotes' | no | no | no | literal text, regexes, awk programs |
| unquoted | yes | yes | yes | almost never |

After an unquoted expansion the shell splits the result on whitespace and then expands any wildcard characters. That is how a harmless filename becomes two arguments:

```bash
file="Incident Report.txt"
touch $file        # creates TWO files: Incident and Report.txt
touch "$file"      # creates one file, as intended

msg="*"
echo $msg          # prints every filename in the directory
echo "$msg"        # prints a literal asterisk
echo '$HOME'       # prints the text $HOME, not your home directory
```

The classic disaster is `rm -rf $dir/*` when `$dir` is empty: it becomes `rm -rf /*`. Defend with quoting and a guard: `rm -rf "${dir:?}"/*`. The rule is simple: quote every expansion unless you can name the reason you need splitting. ShellCheck reports the omission as SC2086.

### Shell variables versus environment variables

A plain assignment creates a shell variable visible only to the current shell. `export` marks it for inheritance by child processes.

```bash
level=high
bash -c 'echo "child sees: [$level]"'   # child sees: []
export level
bash -c 'echo "child sees: [$level]"'   # child sees: [high]

API_TIMEOUT=5 ./enrich.sh               # set for this one command only
printenv | sort                         # list the environment
```

Note the single quotes around the `bash -c` program: they stop the parent shell from expanding `$level` so the child does the expansion. Exported variables are visible to every child process and to `/proc/PID/environ`, so never export secrets you do not need to share.

sections.heading: Positional parameters and reading input
sections.content:
Scripts receive arguments just as commands do. Bash exposes them as special variables.

| Variable | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $0 | name the script was invoked as |
| $1 .. $9 | first to ninth argument; use ${10} for the tenth |
| $# | number of arguments |
| "$@" | all arguments, each kept as a separate word |
| "$*" | all arguments joined into one single word |

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# args.sh
echo "Script : $0"
echo "First  : $1"
echo "Count  : $#"
for a in "$@"; do
  echo "[$a]"
done
```

Running `./args.sh "alpha beta" gamma` prints a count of 2, then `[alpha beta]` and `[gamma]`. The quoted `"$@"` preserves the original argument boundaries, which is almost always what you want. Quoted `"$*"` would produce the single string `alpha beta gamma`, and unquoted `$@` or `$*` would split `alpha beta` into two words. Rule: use `"$@"`.

### Validating arguments

Check the count before using positional parameters, and give optional ones a default:

```bash
if [[ $# -lt 1 ]]; then
  echo "Usage: $0 <logfile> [threshold]" >&2
  exit 2
fi
logfile=$1
threshold=${2:-10}
```

The `>&2` sends the message to standard error so it does not pollute output that another command may be capturing. Exit code 2 is the convention for usage errors.

### shift

`shift` discards `$1` and moves every other argument down by one, decrementing `$#`. It is the standard way to consume arguments in a loop, or to peel off a leading option:

```bash
while [[ $# -gt 0 ]]; do
  echo "Processing: $1"
  shift
done
```

`shift 2` removes two at a time, useful for `-f file` style pairs. For real option parsing with flags, Bash provides the `getopts` builtin; the idea is the same, consume options until the arguments are exhausted.

### Reading input with read

`read` takes a line from standard input and stores it in variables:

```bash
read -r -p "IP to investigate: " ip           # prompt, then wait
read -r -s -p "API key: " key; echo           # -s hides typing
read -r -t 10 -p "Isolate host? [y/N] " ans   # -t gives up after 10 seconds
ans=${ans:-N}
```

Always use `-r`. Without it, backslashes in the input are treated as escape characters and silently eaten, which corrupts Windows paths and regexes. Because `read` reads standard input, it works equally for a person typing and for piped data (`echo 198.51.100.7 | ./lookup.sh`). In automated scripts prefer arguments over prompts: a prompt in a cron job waits forever.

What to ask yourself: what happens if the argument is missing, empty, or contains a space? A script that has an answer to all three is a script you can trust.

sections.heading: Exit codes and testing conditions
sections.content:
### Exit codes

Every command ends with a number from 0 to 255. By convention 0 means success and anything else means failure. The shell stores the last command's status in `$?`.

```bash
grep -q "sshd" /var/log/auth.log
echo $?        # 0 = found, 1 = not found, 2 = error such as missing file

rc=$?          # copy it immediately: the next command overwrites $?
```

Common values: 0 success; 1 general failure; 2 misuse of a command or builtin; 126 found but not executable; 127 command not found; 130 stopped by Ctrl-C; 128+N killed by signal N (137 is SIGKILL). `true` always returns 0 and `false` always returns 1. Your own script ends with the status of its last command unless you call `exit N` explicitly. Exit codes are how cron, CI pipelines and SOAR playbooks decide whether your script worked, so choose them deliberately.

Status drives the control operators: `cmd1 && cmd2` runs the second only on success, and `cmd1 || cmd2` runs it only on failure.

```bash
[[ -d "$outdir" ]] || mkdir -p "$outdir"
grep -q "Failed password" "$log" && echo "Failures present"
```

### test, [ ] and [[ ]]

`test EXPR` and `[ EXPR ]` are the same thing. `[` is a command, not syntax, which is why the spaces inside it are mandatory and why unquoted variables break it. `[[ ... ]]` is a Bash keyword: it does not word-split its variables, supports `&&` and `||` inside, and adds pattern and regex matching. It does not exist in POSIX `sh`.

```bash
name=""
[ $name = "admin" ]      # becomes [ = admin ] : error "unary operator expected"
[ "$name" = "admin" ]    # correct in [ ]
[[ $name == "admin" ]]   # correct in [[ ]], quotes optional on the left
```

| Category | Operator | True when |
|---|---|---|
| String | = or == | strings are equal |
| String | != | strings differ |
| String | -z STR | string is empty |
| String | -n STR | string is not empty |
| String ([[ only) | == pattern | matches glob, e.g. [[ $f == *.log ]] |
| String ([[ only) | =~ regex | matches extended regex |
| Numeric | -eq -ne -lt -le -gt -ge | integer comparison |
| File | -e | path exists |
| File | -f | exists and is a regular file |
| File | -d | exists and is a directory |
| File | -r -w -x | readable, writable, executable by you |
| File | -s | exists and is not empty |

### Pitfalls that bite in practice

Using a string operator on numbers, or the reverse, gives wrong answers without any error:

```bash
a=10; b=9
[[ $a < $b ]] && echo "10 is less than 9?"   # TRUE: compares as text, "1" sorts before "9"
[[ $a -lt $b ]] || echo "correct numeric test"
[ "$a" == 10 ]    # == works in Bash but is not POSIX; use a single = in [ ]
[ $a -eq "abc" ]  # error: integer expression expected
```

Inside `[[ ]]`, an unquoted right-hand side of `==` is a glob pattern, while a quoted one is literal: `[[ $f == "*.log" ]]` matches only a file literally named *.log. For a regex, store it in a variable and leave it unquoted: `[[ $line =~ $re ]]`. Finally, `-z "$var"` and `-n "$var"` are the safe way to test emptiness, and `-f` is false for directories, so pick the file test that matches what you mean.

sections.heading: Conditionals: if/elif/else and case
sections.content:
### if, elif, else, fi

An `if` runs a command and branches on its exit status. The test brackets are just one possible command, which is why you can put any program directly after `if`.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# severity.sh - classify a failed-login count
count=$1

[[ $count =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || { echo "Not a number: $count" >&2; exit 2; }

if [[ $count -ge 100 ]]; then
  echo "CRITICAL"
elif [[ $count -ge 20 ]]; then
  echo "HIGH"
elif [[ $count -ge 5 ]]; then
  echo "MEDIUM"
else
  echo "LOW"
fi
```

The first branch whose condition succeeds runs; the rest are skipped. Every `if` ends with `fi`, and `then` must be on its own line or follow a semicolon. Notice the input validation on the third line: a regex check that the argument is purely digits. Doing this before the numeric comparison prevents the "integer expression expected" error and keeps odd input from reaching later commands.

You can branch directly on a program's result, and negate with `!`:

```bash
if grep -q "Failed password" "$logfile"; then
  echo "Failed logins present"
fi

if ! command -v jq > /dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "jq is required but not installed" >&2
  exit 1
fi
```

Here `command -v` checks whether a tool exists, and `> /dev/null 2>&1` discards both normal output and errors because only the exit status matters. Combine tests with `&&` and `||` inside `[[ ]]`:

```bash
if [[ -f $logfile && -r $logfile && -s $logfile ]]; then
  echo "Log exists, is readable and is not empty"
fi
```

### case and esac

When you compare one value against many patterns, `case` is cleaner than a ladder of `elif`. Each branch is a glob pattern, a closing parenthesis, the commands, and `;;`. A bar separates alternatives, and `*` is the catch-all default.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# portinfo.sh - quick context for a destination port
port=$1
case "$port" in
  22)           echo "SSH: remote admin, common brute-force target" ;;
  23)           echo "Telnet: cleartext, should not be exposed" ;;
  80|443|8080)  echo "Web traffic" ;;
  139|445)      echo "SMB: lateral movement and ransomware spread path" ;;
  3389)         echo "RDP: frequent brute-force and ransomware entry" ;;
  *)            echo "Unclassified port: $port" ;;
esac
```

A second realistic use is dispatching on file type, so one script can open any rotated log:

```bash
case "$file" in
  *.gz)  zcat "$file" ;;
  *.bz2) bzcat "$file" ;;
  *.log) cat "$file" ;;
  *)     echo "Unsupported file type: $file" >&2; exit 1 ;;
esac
```

Remember that `case` uses globs, not regexes, so `*.gz` works but `.*\.gz$` does not. Common mistakes are forgetting a `;;`, forgetting the closing `esac`, and putting the catch-all `*)` first so it swallows everything. Use `if` for different kinds of conditions and `case` for one value with many possibilities.

sections.heading: Loops: for, while, until and reading files
sections.content:
### for loops

A `for` loop assigns each item of a list to a variable in turn.

```bash
for host in web01 web02 db01; do
  echo "Checking $host"
done

for i in {1..5}; do echo "pass $i"; done     # brace expansion
for d in {01..07}; do echo "2026-11-$d"; done # zero padded
```

To process files, loop over a glob, never over the output of `ls`. The glob keeps each filename intact even with spaces, whereas `for f in $(ls)` splits on whitespace.

```bash
for f in /var/log/auth.log*; do
  [[ -e $f ]] || continue          # if nothing matched, f is the literal pattern
  echo "$f: $(wc -l < "$f") lines"
done
```

The C-style form suits counted loops: `for (( i=1; i<=3; i++ )); do echo "attempt $i"; done`.

### while and until

`while` repeats while its command succeeds; `until` repeats until it succeeds.

```bash
attempts=0
while [[ $attempts -lt 3 ]]; do
  echo "Attempt $((attempts + 1))"
  attempts=$((attempts + 1))
done

until ping -c1 -W1 "$host" > /dev/null 2>&1; do
  echo "Waiting for $host..."
  sleep 5
done
```

### Reading a file line by line

This idiom is the backbone of log processing in Bash:

```bash
while IFS= read -r line; do
  echo "LINE: $line"
done < "$file"
```

Each piece has a job. `IFS=` stops `read` from trimming leading and trailing whitespace. `-r` stops backslash handling. The `< "$file"` after `done` feeds the whole loop from the file. `read` returns non-zero at end of input, which ends the loop. To split each line into fields, set IFS for that one command:

```bash
while IFS=, read -r ts user ip; do
  echo "$user logged in from $ip at $ts"
done < events.csv
```

A file whose final line lacks a newline loses that line; add `|| [[ -n $line ]]` to the `while` condition if that matters.

### The pipe subshell trap

The tempting form `cat file | while read ...` runs the loop in a subshell, so variables changed inside vanish afterwards:

```bash
count=0
cat ips.txt | while read -r ip; do count=$((count + 1)); done
echo "$count"      # prints 0

while read -r ip; do count=$((count + 1)); done < ips.txt
echo "$count"      # correct: the loop ran in the current shell

while read -r ip; do count=$((count + 1)); done < <(grep -v '^#' ips.txt)
```

The last form, process substitution, lets you filter first and still keep the loop in the main shell.

### break and continue

`continue` skips to the next iteration and `break` leaves the loop. Together they clean input:

```bash
while IFS= read -r ip; do
  [[ -z $ip ]] && continue            # skip blank lines
  [[ $ip == "#"* ]] && continue       # skip comment lines
  [[ $ip == "END" ]] && break         # stop at a sentinel
  echo "Would block: $ip"
done < blocklist.txt
```

The question for every loop is: what am I iterating over, and could any item contain a space or start with a dash? If so, quote it.

sections.heading: Functions
sections.content:
Functions give a name to a block of commands, so you write the logic once and call it many times. They must be defined before the line that calls them.

```bash
log() {
  local level=$1
  shift
  echo "$(date '+%F %T') [$level] $*" >&2
}

log INFO "Starting analysis of $logfile"
log WARN "Threshold is unusually low"
```

Inside a function, `$1`, `$2`, `$@` and `$#` refer to the function's own arguments, while `$0` is still the script name. Arguments are passed by position with no parentheses at the call site.

### Local variables

By default every variable is global. A function that assigns to a name used elsewhere silently overwrites it. Declare function-internal variables with `local`.

```bash
total=100
bad()  { total=0; }        # clobbers the caller's variable
good() { local total=0; }  # private to the function
bad;  echo "$total"        # 0
total=100
good; echo "$total"        # 100
```

### return versus echo and capture

These two mechanisms carry different kinds of result. `return N` sets the exit status, a number from 0 to 255, and is meant for yes/no answers that `if` can test. To produce actual data such as a string, print it with `echo` and capture it with `$(...)`.

```bash
is_private_ip() {
  local ip=$1
  [[ $ip =~ ^(10\.|192\.168\.|172\.(1[6-9]|2[0-9]|3[01])\.) ]]
}

if is_private_ip "$src"; then
  echo "internal source"
else
  echo "external source"
fi

email_domain() {
  local email=$1
  echo "${email#*@}"
}

domain=$(email_domain "analyst@example.org")
echo "$domain"       # example.org
```

In `is_private_ip` there is no explicit `return`: a function returns the status of its last command, here the regex test. Writing `return` with a string, as in `return "yes"`, is an error because only integers are allowed.

### Pitfalls

- **Logging inside captured functions.** Anything a function prints to standard output becomes part of `$(...)`. Send diagnostics to standard error (`>&2`) so the captured value stays clean.
- **local hides failures.** In `local out=$(some_command)` the exit status you see is that of `local`, which is always 0, so the failure of `some_command` is lost. Split it: `local out` on one line, then `out=$(some_command)` on the next. ShellCheck flags this as SC2155.
- **exit versus return.** `return` leaves the function; `exit` ends the entire script. Inside `$(...)` an `exit` only ends the subshell that is capturing the output.
- **Trailing newlines.** `$(...)` strips trailing newlines from captured text, which is normally helpful.

Good function design for SOC work: one job per function, validate arguments at the top, report errors to stderr, and return a meaningful status. A small library of functions such as `is_private_ip`, `log` and `require_tool` can be sourced from many scripts.

sections.heading: Arithmetic, arrays and here-documents
sections.content:
### Integer arithmetic

Bash does integer math with `$(( ))`, which yields a value, and `(( ))`, which evaluates and sets an exit status. Inside them, variable names need no dollar sign.

```bash
a=7; b=3
echo $((a + b)) $((a * b)) $((a / b)) $((a % b)) $((a ** 2))   # 10 21 2 1 49
total=$((total + 1))

failed=40; total=200
echo "$((failed * 100 / total))% failed"      # 20% failed

if (( failed > 25 )); then echo "over threshold"; fi
```

In `(( ))` you can use C-style comparison operators (`>`, `==`, `<=`) safely on numbers. Division truncates, and there are no floating-point numbers; for fractions use `awk` or `bc`: `echo "scale=2; 7/3" | bc`. One trap: `((count++))` returns exit status 1 when the expression evaluates to 0, which aborts a script running under `set -e`. Write `count=$((count + 1))` instead.

### Indexed arrays

An array holds a list without the splitting problems of a space-separated string. Indexes start at 0.

```bash
hosts=(web01 web02 "db 01")
echo "${hosts[0]}"            # web01
echo "${#hosts[@]}"           # 3 elements
hosts+=(mail01)               # append
for h in "${hosts[@]}"; do echo "host: $h"; done
echo "${hosts[@]:1:2}"        # slice: two elements starting at index 1

mapfile -t lines < /etc/hosts # read a file into an array, one line per element
```

Quote `"${hosts[@]}"` for the same reason you quote `"$@"`: it keeps `db 01` as a single element. Associative arrays (Bash 4 and newer) map string keys to values, which is ideal for counting:

```bash
declare -A seen
seen[203.0.113.45]=3
seen[198.51.100.7]=1
seen[198.51.100.7]=$(( ${seen[198.51.100.7]} + 1 ))
for k in "${!seen[@]}"; do echo "$k -> ${seen[$k]}"; done
```

`${!seen[@]}` lists the keys. Associative arrays do not exist in the Bash 3.2 that macOS ships, so check `bash --version` before relying on them.

### Here-documents and here-strings

A here-document feeds a multi-line block to a command's standard input until it sees the closing delimiter alone on a line.

```bash
cat <<EOF
Report for $(hostname)
Generated: $(date -u +%FT%TZ)
EOF

cat > /tmp/patterns.txt <<'EOF'
Failed password
Invalid user
EOF
grep -F -f /tmp/patterns.txt /var/log/auth.log
```

With an unquoted delimiter (`<<EOF`) variables and substitutions are expanded. With a quoted delimiter (`<<'EOF'`) the text is taken literally, which is what you want for regexes and for generating other scripts. Using `<<-EOF` strips leading tab characters so you can indent the block.

A here-string, `<<<`, supplies a single string as input. It is a clean way to split a value into variables without a pipe, and it avoids the subshell trap from the loops section:

```bash
read -r user ip <<< "alice 203.0.113.9"
echo "$user connected from $ip"

grep -c "Failed" <<< "$output"
```

sections.heading: A worked SOC script: failed SSH logins per source IP
sections.content:
The task: read an SSH authentication log, count failed logins per source IP, and flag every IP above a threshold. It uses the log lines sshd writes, such as:

```
Nov  2 03:14:07 web01 sshd[2211]: Failed password for invalid user admin from 203.0.113.45 port 51822 ssh2
Nov  2 03:14:09 web01 sshd[2213]: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.45 port 51830 ssh2
Nov  2 03:15:41 web01 sshd[2290]: Accepted publickey for deploy from 198.51.100.7 port 40112 ssh2
```

Here is the whole script (requires Bash 4.4 or newer):

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# failed-ssh.sh - count failed SSH logins per source IP, flag heavy hitters
# Usage: ./failed-ssh.sh <auth.log> [threshold]
set -euo pipefail

[[ $# -ge 1 ]] || { echo "Usage: $0 <auth.log> [threshold]" >&2; exit 2; }
logfile=$1
threshold=${2:-10}

[[ -r $logfile ]] || { echo "Cannot read: $logfile" >&2; exit 1; }
[[ $threshold =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || { echo "Threshold must be a number" >&2; exit 2; }

declare -A fails
re='Failed (password|publickey) for (invalid user )?([^ ]+) from ([0-9.]+)'

while IFS= read -r line; do
  if [[ $line =~ $re ]]; then
    ip=${BASH_REMATCH[4]}
    fails[$ip]=$(( ${fails[$ip]:-0} + 1 ))
  fi
done < "$logfile"

mapfile -t flagged < <(
  for ip in "${!fails[@]}"; do
    (( fails[$ip] > threshold )) && echo "$ip ${fails[$ip]}"
  done | sort -k2,2nr
)

if (( ${#flagged[@]} == 0 )); then
  echo "No IP exceeded $threshold failures (${#fails[@]} distinct IPs seen)"
  exit 0
fi

printf '%-16s %6s\n' "IP" "FAILED"
for entry in "${flagged[@]}"; do
  read -r ip count <<< "$entry"
  printf '%-16s %6d\n' "$ip" "$count"
done
echo "${#flagged[@]} IP(s) exceeded $threshold failures"
exit 3
```

### Line by line

- **set -euo pipefail** makes the script stop on errors, unset variables and failed pipeline stages (details below).
- **The two guard lines** show usage and exit 2 if no log file was given. `threshold=${2:-10}` makes the second argument optional with a default of 10.
- **Input validation** checks the file is readable (`-r`) and the threshold is all digits, so later arithmetic cannot fail on bad input.
- **declare -A fails** creates an associative array mapping IP to count.
- **The re variable** holds the regex in single quotes, and it is used unquoted in `=~`. Group 4 is the source IP; group 3 is the username, whether or not the line says "invalid user".
- **The while loop** reads with `IFS= read -r`, tests each line against the regex, and `BASH_REMATCH[4]` yields the captured IP. `${fails[$ip]:-0}` treats a first-seen IP as zero, so the increment works under `set -u`.
- **mapfile with process substitution** runs the filter loop in a subshell, prints `IP count` pairs above the threshold, sorts numerically descending on field 2, and loads the lines into the array `flagged`.
- **The report section** exits 0 if nothing was flagged. Otherwise it prints a header, splits each entry with a here-string, and formats columns with `printf`.
- **exit 3** is a deliberate convention: 0 means clean and 3 means findings, so a scheduler or SOAR job can branch on the result.

Example run: `./failed-ssh.sh /var/log/auth.log 10` prints the header, one row per flagged IP such as `203.0.113.45` with its count, and a summary line. A pipeline of grep, awk, sort and uniq -c gives a useful cross-check of your counts and is much faster on multi-gigabyte logs, since Bash loops process lines slowly. Remember that RHEL-family systems log to /var/log/secure instead.

### Robustness and ShellCheck

`set -e` exits on any failing command, `set -u` treats an unset variable as an error, and `set -o pipefail` makes a pipeline fail if any stage fails, not just the last. Together they turn silent corruption into loud failure. They have sharp edges: `grep` returns 1 when nothing matches, which under pipefail can abort a pipeline, so write `grep ... || true` where no match is acceptable. Commands inside `if` conditions and `||` lists are exempt from `-e`.

Before deploying, run `bash -n script.sh` for a syntax check, `bash -x script.sh` to trace each command, and `shellcheck script.sh` to lint it. ShellCheck catches the bugs from this lesson: SC2086 (unquoted expansion), SC2155 (local masking a failure), SC2164 (cd without a failure check) and SC2046 (unquoted command substitution). Treat its warnings as defects, not suggestions.

quiz.question: A cleanup script sets file="Incident Report.txt" and then runs: rm $file. The directory contains both "Incident Report.txt" and an unrelated file named "Report.txt". What happens?

options.label: Only "Incident Report.txt" is deleted, because the variable holds the whole name
rm receives two words, so it fails on "Incident" and deletes the unrelated "Report.txt"
Bash stops with a syntax error before running rm
rm deletes "Incident Report.txt" but asks for confirmation first

quiz.explanation: Unquoted expansion is split on whitespace, so rm sees Incident and Report.txt as separate arguments. It reports an error for the nonexistent Incident and deletes the unrelated Report.txt, leaving the intended file in place. The claim that the variable keeps the whole name is wrong because splitting happens after expansion, not before. There is no syntax error, since the command is valid, just wrong. rm does not prompt unless you pass -i, and prompting would not fix the wrong target anyway. The fix is rm -- "$file".

quiz.question: A script is run as: ./check.sh "alpha beta" gamma. Which loop prints exactly two lines, [alpha beta] and [gamma], one per original argument?

options.label: for a in $*; do echo "[$a]"; done
for a in "$*"; do echo "[$a]"; done
for a in "$@"; do echo "[$a]"; done
for a in $@; do echo "[$a]"; done

quiz.explanation: Quoted "$@" expands to each argument as its own word, preserving the space inside "alpha beta". Unquoted $* and unquoted $@ both split on whitespace and would print three lines: [alpha], [beta], [gamma]. Quoted "$*" joins everything into one string, so it prints a single line [alpha beta gamma]. Use "$@" whenever you want to pass arguments along intact.

quiz.question: A script contains: a=10; b=9; if [[ $a < $b ]]; then echo "a is smaller"; fi. What does it print and why?

options.label: It prints "a is smaller", because < inside [[ ]] compares strings and the text "10" sorts before "9"
It prints nothing, because 10 is greater than 9 numerically
It fails with "integer expression expected"
It redirects input from a file named 9

quiz.explanation: Inside [[ ]] the < operator is a lexicographic string comparison, and the character 1 sorts before 9, so the test is true. Expecting no output assumes a numeric comparison, which would need -lt or (( a < b )). The integer-expression error comes from [ ] with -eq style operators on non-numbers, not from this test. Redirection would only happen with a bare [ a < b ] outside the double-bracket keyword, and that is not the case here.

quiz.question: A script runs: count=0; cat ips.txt | while read -r ip; do count=$((count + 1)); done; echo "$count". The file has 40 lines but the script prints 0. What is the cause?

options.label: cat cannot be used with read, so the loop never starts
Arithmetic requires the let command, so the increment fails silently
read without IFS= discards every line it receives
The piped loop runs in a subshell, so the increment changes a copy that vanishes when the loop ends

quiz.explanation: Each side of a pipe runs in its own subshell, so the loop increments its own copy of count and the parent shell still sees 0. The fix is to feed the loop by redirection (done < ips.txt) or process substitution. cat and read work together fine; the loop does start. The $(( )) syntax is valid arithmetic and needs no let. Omitting IFS= only affects leading and trailing whitespace trimming, not whether lines are read.

quiz.question: A script uses set -euo pipefail and contains: failed=$(grep "Failed password" auth.log | wc -l). On a clean log with no matches, the script exits silently at this line. Why?

options.label: wc -l returns an error when given zero lines
grep exits with status 1 on no match, pipefail makes that the pipeline's status, and -e aborts the script
set -u treats the empty result as an unset variable and prints an error
Command substitution is not allowed when set -e is active

quiz.explanation: grep returns 1 when nothing matches. Without pipefail the pipeline would take wc's status of 0, but with pipefail the failing stage determines the status, and set -e then stops the script with no message. wc -l simply prints 0 for empty input and succeeds. set -u only complains about unset variables, and failed is assigned (to an empty string at worst), and it would print an error rather than exit silently. Command substitution is perfectly legal under set -e. Use grep -c ... || true, or grep ... || true inside the pipeline, when no match is acceptable.
